paragraphs.heading: Choosing one thing or another
paragraphs.text: The rule of sum, also called the addition principle, is one of the basic principles of counting in combinatorics. It handles choices where you pick one option or another, but never both. Say one action can be done in A ways and a different action in B ways. If the two cannot both happen at once, you have A + B ways to choose one of them. Put this simply, it is an intuitive idea.

paragraphs.heading: A day of shopping
paragraphs.text: Imagine someone who will shop at just one store today, in either the north or the south part of town. In the north, the options are a mall, a furniture store or a jewelry store, which makes 3 ways. In the south, the options are a clothing store or a shoe store, which makes 2 ways. Adding the two groups gives 3 + 2 = 5 shops where the day's shopping could end up.

paragraphs.heading: The rule in the language of sets
paragraphs.text: The same idea can be written with sets. Two sets are called disjoint when they have no elements in common. For disjoint sets A and B, the principle says |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B|, on the condition that nothing lies in both sets. Seen through this equation, the addition principle turns out to be a statement belonging to set theory.

paragraphs.heading: More than two groups
paragraphs.text: The rule is not limited to two sets; it stretches to cover several. For sets S₁, S₂, …, Sₙ that are pairwise disjoint, the principle gives |S₁| + |S₂| + ⋯ + |Sₙ| = | S₁ ∪ S₂ ∪ ⋯ ∪ Sₙ |. This longer version can be proved from the two-set addition principle by induction on n.

paragraphs.heading: Counting what is left over
paragraphs.text: The rule also gives a quick result about a set inside a bigger one. Take a finite set S, and another set A with A ⊂ S. Then |A^c| = |S| − |A|. The proof is short: by the addition principle, |A^c| + |A| = |S|, and subtracting |A| from both sides gives the result.

paragraphs.heading: A building block for other rules
paragraphs.text: Simple as it is, the addition principle can be used to prove other counting results. One of them is Pascal's rule, which can be proved combinatorially with its help. It can even be used to prove the multiplication principle.
